title: Where Rivers Drop Their Load
question: What happens when a river reaches the end of its course?
hook: A river carries sand for hundreds of kilometres, then lets much of it go in one place.
idea: At its mouth a river slows and drops its sediment, building landforms, and how its water enters depends on whether it is heavier or lighter than the water it meets.

beats.prompt: A fresh-water river flows into the salty sea. Where does the river water go at first?

choices.label: It sinks to the seabed
choices.feedback: River water only plunges when it is denser than the water it meets; fresh water is usually lighter than seawater.

choices.label: It stops dead at the shoreline
choices.feedback: The river keeps moving into the sea; the question is whether it flows over or under the seawater.

beats.explain: Fresh river water is usually lighter than seawater, so it spreads out along the surface as an overflow.

beats.prompt: Sort each outcome by whether the river water is denser or lighter than the water it enters.
items: Typical of fresh water entering the sea
beats.explain: Relative density decides the path: denser river water dives under, lighter river water rides on top.

beats.prompt: Match each English town to the river whose mouth it sits at.
beats.explain: Many places in the United Kingdom are named for their spot at a river's mouth.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A river reaches the sea and its current slows down.
Slower water can carry less sediment.
So the river picks up extra sediment at its mouth.
That sediment builds landforms like deltas, sand bars and spits.
beats.explain: Slower water carries less, so the river drops sediment at its mouth instead of picking more up.
